blindSummary:
This country poses severe risk to trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and gender-based violence overall is extreme — among the world's highest documented rates. Its two largest cities are dangerous for everyone; customary community-justice dynamics and police brutality hit marginalised people hard. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and violence driven by accusations of harmful spiritual practices shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in its world region.
blindOutOfScope: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.

International human-rights organisation (Jan 2009): report on a country where violence against women is rampant - documents widespread gender-based violence in this country, the context of impunity that also affects sexual and gender minorities.

A foreign public broadcaster (Oct 2014): a coastal village on the outskirts of this country's largest city (notably the home of roughly half of the national team) is a safe haven for gay and trans people in a country where homosexuality is illegal.

Foreign broadsheet (Jan 2017): a rights group said this country had failed to act on corruption and police violence or protect women and children - a scathing assessment that also covers a wealthy neighbour's offshore immigration detention run here.

Foreign women's-interest publication (Nov 2018): feature on a village in this country that serves as a refuge for its LGBT community - an openly gay 24-year-old remembers thugs pelting him with abuse, stones and bottles; the coastal settlement offers refuge where gay sex is illegal and stigma and violence are widespread.
